A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Hvt-UCB research. The main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices are readable and support comparison despite substantial reformatting.

before.justification: Section 6 and Figures 1–2 report original synthetic bandit experiments measuring cumulative regret and runtime under Student's t and Gaussian noise.

after.justification: Section 5 retains those experiments, and Appendix E reports additional original experiments with different noise distributions, varying noise scales and changing arm sets.

M1.justification: The Huber loss, OMD estimator, normalization and robustification schedules, confidence radius and UCB selection rule remain the same in Equations (7)–(11) and Algorithm 1. Distinguishing the intermediate projected-gradient iterate with a tilde clarifies notation without changing the procedure.

E1.justification: Appendix E substantially expands the synthetic evaluation beyond the retained Student's t and Gaussian experiments. It adds asymmetric Pareto, Lomax and Fisk noise, randomly varying noise scales, and changing sets of available arms, testing materially different input and decision conditions.

E2.justification: OFUL, CRTM, CRMM and Heavy-OFUL remain the evaluated comparator set. However, Appendix E.3 introduces an adaptation of CRMM for changing arm sets: unavailable repeated pulls are replaced by the closest available arms. The original comparisons remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The original d=2, 50-arm, 18,000-round experiments retain their settings. Appendix E adds substantial evaluation protocols: specified asymmetric-noise parameters, Student's t noise with df=1.7 and random logarithmic scaling, and per-round subsets of 40 or 30 of 50 arms with regret measured against the best available arm.

E4.justification: Figures 3–5 add a systematic robustness and sensitivity suite examining noise asymmetry, noise-scale variation and changing arm availability. The fixed/40-arm/30-arm comparison directly probes the consequences of repeated-pulling requirements, which v1 discussed without this experimental analysis.

E5.justification: The original experiments still report averages over 10 independent trials and variance shading. Appendices E.1 and E.3 newly specify averages over five independent trials for their added experiments; this does not establish any reduction in the original experiments' repetitions.

E6.justification: Figures 1–2 retain their curves and runtime values. Nine new panels in Figures 3–5 report performance under additional conditions, including competitive Hvt-UCB results with asymmetric noise, advantages for Hvt-UCB and Heavy-OFUL under varying noise scales, and deterioration of CRMM when arm availability changes.

T1.justification: Hvt-UCB's assumptions, guarantees and proofs in Appendices A–D remain substantively unchanged. Section 2 nevertheless changes the stated dependence on the nonlinearity parameter from κ^-1 to κ in the quoted GLM-UCB, OL2M and CRTM/CRMM regret bounds, without specifying a compensating redefinition.

C1.justification: The central claims of one-pass computation and optimal, instance-dependent regret are retained. The conclusion narrows the extension claim from saying the method can be extended to online MDPs and adaptive control to saying it has the potential to be extended.

C2.justification: v2 explains the runtime disadvantage relative to least-squares baselines through Hvt-UCB's projection step and adds interpretations of CRMM's behavior under asymmetric noise and changing arms. Remark 1 further explains normalization's role relative to other Huber approaches, while the discussion qualifies direct applicability to MDPs.

D1.justification: Appendix E adds implementation information for the new experiments, including scipy.stats distributions and shape parameters, the noise-multiplier sampling rule, arm-subset construction and CRMM's nearest-available-arm workaround. These are new experimental details, rather than changes to the retained implementation.

R1.justification: v2 extends discussion to low-rank Huber bandits, TERM, offline reweighting methods, gradient-variation techniques and parameter-free heavy-tailed bandits. Remark 1 sharpens distinctions from other Huber estimators. The central positioning against Heavy-OFUL remains; Huang and Li–Sun publication updates refer to the same works.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the introductory challenges and conclusion, moves Experiments before Discussion, adds Remark 1, acknowledgements and an impact statement, and removes the introductory notation paragraph. Most methodological exposition and proof text remain closely matched.

P2.justification: The main text and references change from a single-column manuscript to an ICML two-column layout. Figures 1–2 and Algorithm 1 are resized and repositioned, Table 1 is reformatted, and Appendix E adds three new three-panel figures.

improvement.justification: v2 adds relevant robustness tests and more appropriately tentative extension claims. However, Appendices E.1 and E.2 report ε=1.49 and ε=1.69, conflicting with the retained requirement ε∈(0,1]. The PDFs do not establish whether these are reporting errors or actual configurations, leaving the reliability of the added empirical support—and the net quality improvement—uncertain.
